title: Text structure Practice 2
description: 4 short texts - 8 focused text structure questions
subject: rla
passage:
TEXT A - Flood Alerts

Residents near a creek often received warnings after water had already covered one road. The town installed an upstream sensor linked to automatic text alerts. During later storms, messages arrived earlier.

TEXT B - Study Pods

The library offers open tables for group work, enclosed pods for calls, and silent desks along the back wall. Each space is described by noise level and typical use.

TEXT C - Pavement and Runoff

Paved surfaces prevent much rain from soaking into soil. More water then flows across the surface into drains, which can raise peak runoff during intense storms.

TEXT D - Market Options

A market can extend hours every evening or only on Fridays and Saturdays. The report compares staffing cost, expected customer traffic, and vendor interest before recommending weekend evenings.

questions.prompt: Which text structure best describes this passage?
questions.explanation: The passage introduces late flood warnings as a problem, then presents an upstream sensor and automatic alerts as the response.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: cause / effect only
options.whyWrong: The sensor affects warning time, but the passage is framed around a problem and a response.

options.text: problem / solution
sequence / process
options.whyWrong: The events have an order, but the text is not teaching a procedure.

options.text: compare / contrast
options.whyWrong: It does not weigh two alert systems using parallel criteria.

questions.prompt: How does that structure help develop the passage?
questions.explanation: Problem/solution organization helps readers see why the system was introduced and what changed afterward.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: It mainly explains the mechanical steps for installing a creek sensor.
options.whyWrong: Installation details are not the focus.

options.text: It compares residents who receive alerts with residents who do not.
options.whyWrong: No parallel groups of residents are compared.

options.text: It links a timing problem with the new alert system and the improvement observed during later storms.
It classifies different kinds of storms by severity.
options.whyWrong: Storm categories are not presented.

questions.prompt: Which text structure best describes this passage?
questions.explanation: The library groups spaces by type and describes each according to noise level and typical use.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: compare / contrast leading to a recommendation
options.whyWrong: Readers can compare the spaces, but the passage primarily organizes them into categories and describes each.

options.text: sequence / process
options.whyWrong: The spaces are not steps in an activity.

options.text: cause / effect
options.whyWrong: No causal chain organizes the descriptions.

options.text: classification / description

questions.prompt: How does that structure help develop the passage?
questions.explanation: Classification makes the options easy to distinguish by their defining features.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: Grouping the spaces by type helps readers match a setting to the activity and noise level they need.
It shows how using one space causes another space to become quieter.
options.whyWrong: The categories are described independently; one does not cause another.

options.text: It tells readers the order in which they must use the library spaces.
options.whyWrong: The categories are choices, not steps.

options.text: It argues that enclosed pods are better than every other study space.
options.whyWrong: The passage describes different uses rather than declaring one category best.

questions.prompt: Which text structure best describes this passage?
questions.explanation: The passage explains how pavement reduces infiltration, which increases surface flow and can raise peak runoff.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: cause / effect
problem / solution
options.whyWrong: No response or solution is proposed.

options.text: classification / description
options.whyWrong: The details form a causal chain rather than separate categories.

options.text: compare / contrast
options.whyWrong: The passage does not compare two surfaces using parallel criteria.

questions.prompt: How does that structure help develop the passage?
questions.explanation: Cause-and-effect structure connects reduced infiltration to surface flow and higher peak runoff.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: It lists several independent features of pavement without explaining how they relate.
options.whyWrong: The sentences explicitly connect one condition to the next.

options.text: It gives instructions for measuring runoff during a storm.
options.whyWrong: No measurement procedure is described.

options.text: It weighs the advantages of pavement against the advantages of soil.
options.whyWrong: The text focuses on causal effects of pavement.

options.text: The organization traces how one physical change can produce a chain of later runoff effects.

questions.prompt: Which text structure best describes this passage?
questions.explanation: The report compares two scheduling options on staffing cost, customer traffic, and vendor interest before recommending one.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: sequence / process
options.whyWrong: The options are alternatives, not steps.

options.text: compare / contrast leading to a recommendation
cause / effect only
options.whyWrong: The passage evaluates alternatives rather than tracing one causal chain.

options.text: classification only
options.whyWrong: The options are not merely grouped; they are compared using shared criteria to support a decision.

questions.prompt: How does that structure help develop the passage?
questions.explanation: The comparison makes the recommendation traceable to staffing, traffic, and vendor-interest evidence.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: It shows that extending hours every evening directly causes vendors to lose interest.
options.whyWrong: The passage compares expected effects; it does not state this causal conclusion.

options.text: It explains the chronological steps required to change market hours.
options.whyWrong: Implementation steps are not the organizing focus.

options.text: Using the same criteria for both scheduling options creates a reasoned basis for the recommendation.
It describes both options but deliberately avoids evaluating them.
options.whyWrong: The report compares them in order to make a recommendation.
